title: POC VPC Networking deep-dive: peering & private endpoints
content:
Context:
This note captures the solutions-eng POC design options we walked through with Customer X on 2024-11-01 and in the 2024-12-03 follow-up workshop. The goal: enable Redwood Private (control plane in our SaaS/VPC or customer-managed control plane) to talk to the customer’s model-serving VPCs, while satisfying their security constraints (no internet egress from model VPCs, auditability, fixed egress IPs for allowlisting, and private DNS resolution).

Scope:
- Cloud providers: primary focus AWS, brief alternatives for GCP/Azure.
- Connectivity patterns: VPC Peering, Transit Hub (Transit Gateway / VPC Network Peering equivalents), PrivateLink / Interface Endpoints, Private Service Connect.
- DNS resolution options and split-horizon/private hosted zones.
- Ingress/Egress strategies: internal load balancers, NAT static egress, proxies.
- Operational controls: routing, security groups, NACLs, logging, certs, KMS/HSM traffic considerations.

Topologies we considered (summary):
1) Hub-and-spoke (recommended for medium+ scale):
   - Hub = central networking VPC owned by customer or Redwood-managed VPC (depending on contract).
   - Spokes = customer app/model VPCs + Redwood runtime VPCs.
   - Connectivity via AWS Transit Gateway (TGW) or GCP Shared VPC/Cloud Router.
   - Advantages: centralized egress controls, NATs, monitoring, easier cross-account PrivateLink.
   - Tradeoffs: requires TGW quota & transit attachments; more initial setup.

2) Direct VPC Peering mesh (small scale, simple):
   - Pairwise peering between Redwood VPC and each model VPC.
   - Advantages: simple routing, lower cost for 1–2 VPCs.
   - Tradeoffs: does not support transitive routing; scales poorly with N VPCs.

3) PrivateLink / Interface Endpoints (best for SaaS control plane to customer):
   - Expose Redwood control-plane API as interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) into customer VPC or hub VPC.
   - For customer-hosted runtime, create interface endpoint in their VPC pointing at Redwood NLB in our account or use endpoint services on their side.
   - Advantages: no route table changes for many spoke-to-service connections, strong access control via endpoint policies.
   - Tradeoffs: extra ENI overhead, per-endpoint cost.

Detailed design notes / checklist:
A. CIDR planning & overlap detection
   - Require customer to provide all VPC CIDRs (including peered accounts) early. Overlapping CIDRs kill peering/transit.
   - Recommended minimal CIDR blocks: reserve /24 per cluster or service for future peering.

B. Choice: TGW (hub) vs peering mesh
   - If customer has >3 VPCs or expects growth, recommend TGW.
   - If low count (1–2) and no centralized security needed, peering is fine.

C. DNS model (critical)
   - AWS: use Route 53 Private Hosted Zones (PHZ) with VPC association for split-horizon. For hub designs, associate PHZs with spoke VPCs or create Resolver rules.
   - Option: Route53 Resolver inbound endpoints in hub VPC to let Redwood resolve customer-private names (or vice versa).
   - For AWS PrivateLink, use AWS provided Private DNS name option to allow standard hostnames to resolve to the interface endpoint.
   - GCP: use Cloud DNS private zones with VPC peering/Shared VPC; Private Service Connect for service exposure.
   - Key operational point: ensure the chosen DNS path preserves TLS cert hostnames used by Redwood endpoints — if TLS terminations are in customer VPC, cert SANs must match internal hostnames.

D. Ingress patterns for Redwood -> customer runtimes
   - If Redwood initiates connections into customer-only resources: prefer PrivateLink (interface endpoint service) exposed by customer to Redwood. Customer runs NLB in front of their control-plane API or runtime orchestration endpoint and exposes as Endpoint Service.
   - Alternatively, Redwood runs an NLB (in Redwood account) and customer creates interface endpoints pointing to it. For hosted control-plane, this is the common pattern.

E. Egress / internet access from model VPCs
   - Two common policies: 1) no internet egress allowed, 2) controlled egress via NAT/proxy with allowlist.
   - For static egress IP requirement: implement NAT Gateway(s) with Elastic IPs in a NAT subnet in the hub; use source/destination checks and centralized route table to send 0.0.0.0/0 via NAT.
   - Alternative (cost-sensitive): run a small fleet of egress proxies (Squid/Envoy) behind an internal ALB with static egress IPs (via NAT GW or a small set of EIPs attached to a Network Load Balancer + IP address mapping). Provides more control (TLS termination, request inspection).

F. Security groups, NACLs, and endpoint policies
   - Principle: tight SGs allow only specific ports and Redwood control-plane CIDRs. Implement least privilege.
   - For PrivateLink, set endpoint policy to restrict which principals (Redwood account or specific role) can use the endpoint.
   - Use route table tagging + IAM org policies to reduce accidental cross-VPC exposure.

G. KMS/HSM and secrets access
   - If customer KMS must be used from Redwood runtime (e.g., key wrapping), ensure role-based cross-account access and KMS key policies allow Redwood account ARN(s). Consider VPC endpoints for KMS if supported in the cloud.
   - For HSM over network: ensure dedicated connectivity (Direct Connect or VPN) and coordinate with compliance.

H. Observability & flow logs
   - Enable VPC Flow Logs at the hub and spoke levels; ship to a centralized S3/CloudWatch/Logging project.
   - Capture ALB/NLB access logs and PrivateLink usage metrics.
   - Redwood will provide tracing hooks — ensure endpoints allow inbound tracing ports or use a dedicated agent that proxies traces to Redwood observability.

I. IAM, service accounts, and cross-account roles
   - Prefer cross-account IAM roles with granular permissions (AssumeRole) instead of long-lived credentials.
   - Document role ARNs and required trust policy changes as part of the onboarding checklist.

J. Latency and path optimisation
   - For latency-sensitive model invocation, colocate Redwood runtime in the same region as customer VPC/hub. Use cross-AZ attachments only when necessary.

Operational checklist (pre-workshop / pre-POC):
- [ ] Customer provides list of VPC IDs, CIDRs, Account IDs, Regions, and existing TGW/Peering attachments.
- [ ] Confirm whether customer allows new Transit Gateway attachments or PrivateLink endpoints.
- [ ] Confirm required static egress IPs and allowlist processes.
- [ ] Confirm whether DNS private zones exist and provide zone names+records to validate.
- [ ] Agree on audit/log retention and location (S3 bucket / logging project).
- [ ] Identify the owner for route table, SG, and NACL changes.
- [ ] Exchange IAM role ARNs for cross-account assume-role.

Ports & services matrix (common):
- Control-plane API (Redwood <-> Customer): TCP 443 (TLS) default.
- Health / metrics endpoints: TCP 8080/9100 internal only (ask customer).
- SSH (if required for debug): TCP 22 from explicit bastion SG only.
- Model-serving ports: application-defined (e.g., 5000, 8080) — close by default.
- PrivateLink: uses ENI traffic, no extra ports beyond 443 unless the service exposes others.

Troubleshooting guide (quick):
1) DNS failures: check Resolver rules, PHZ associations, PrivateLink DNS settings. Use dig + server=@<resolver-ip>.
2) Connectivity but TLS handshake fail: verify internal CN/SAN and SNI behavior; confirm certs valid for private names.
3) Traffic dropped: inspect SGs, NACLs, and route tables for blackhole routes or missing routes to TGW.
4) Intermittent timeouts: look at ENI limits on PrivateLink, throttling on NLB, and per-connection NAT timeouts.

Workshop agenda (recommended 2 hours):
- 0:00–0:10 Introductions & objectives
- 0:10–0:25 Customer current state: VPCs, CIDRs, connectivity, ownership
- 0:25–0:50 Walk through recommended topology (hub vs peering) and DNS options
- 0:50–1:15 Egress patterns & allowlist strategy (NAT vs proxy)
- 1:15–1:35 Operational controls: IAM, monitoring, flow logs, KMS access
- 1:35–1:55 Implementation plan + timelines + responsibilities
- 1:55–2:00 Action items and next steps

Open questions for Customer X (to resolve before demo):
- Do you have an existing TGW or prefer peering?
- Which AWS account should own the hub VPC? (customer-owned recommended for strict data isolation)
- Required RTO/RPO for control-plane vs runtime events?
- Any regulatory constraints on routing through third-party accounts (e.g., Redwood-managed hub)?
- Do you require traffic inspection (proxy) or is simple NAT + allowlist enough?

Implementation snippets (AWS examples we will hand over):
- Route53 Resolver inbound endpoint in hub for resolving .internal zones from Redwood control plane and vice versa.
- Create Interface VPC Endpoint (com.amazonaws.<region>.logs) for cross-account logging ingestion if central logging required.
- Endpoint service + NLB if customer exposes runtime as ManagedEndpoint: create acceptance rule for Redwood account.

Decision / Recommendation summary (POC):
- For POC with Customer X: use hub-and-spoke with customer-owned hub VPC and Transit Gateway. Host NAT + centralized logging in hub. Use PrivateLink for the control-plane API exposure and Reserve a small internal ALB/NLB for internal health checks.
- DNS: use Route53 PHZ associated to hub and spoke VPCs; create Resolver inbound endpoint for cross-account resolution.
- Static egress IPs: NAT Gateway(s) with Elastic IPs in hub. If cost is a concern, run a cheap egress proxy cluster behind NAT.

Action items (post-workshop):
- [Jordan Kim] Draft step-by-step runbook for TGW attachment and PHZ associations (due 2024-11-13).
- [Maya Singh] Provision test NAT GW + Elastic IPs in staging hub and share test egress IPs (due 2024-11-20).
- [Customer X network owner] Provide CIDR list and permission to create TGW attachment.
- [Luca Romero] Prepare PrivateLink endpoint service acceptance policy template.

Appendix: short notes on GCP & Azure equivalents
- GCP: consider Private Service Connect for service exposure and use Cloud Router + Cloud NAT in a Shared VPC or hub project. DNS via Cloud DNS private zones and DNS peering.
- Azure: use Private Link (Private Endpoint) and Virtual WAN / Hub for hub-and-spoke. Use Azure Firewall or NAT gateway for static egress IPs.

If we proceed with the recommended hub+TGW approach I will produce an implementation runbook with exact CLI/console steps, Terraform snippets, and pre-filled policy documents for PrivateLink endpoint policies and Route53 Resolver rules.

Notes-to-self and variants tried during workshop (raw):
- We attempted a quick demo of cross-account PrivateLink where the customer exposed an NLB and we created an interface endpoint from our account. Acceptance workflow was manual — need to include an automation path.
- Customer asked about avoiding TGW cost; offered peering + one hop self-managed proxy for up to 3 VPCs.
- KMS access: customer insisted on not sharing key material; proposed envelope encryption where Redwood holds only wrapped keys and customer KMS unwrap is done inside customer network.

End of note.
